doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

title: 'Insomnia', Paul Clarvis's feel, and playing alone
summary: 'Insomnia' was written after a 3 A.M. wake-up; the live version with Paul Clarvis swings; she enjoys solo saxophone.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Beautifully said. Thank you. The other piece I was going to ask about, “Insomnia.” I wonder if you have trouble sleeping. That’s not my question.

Sometimes the titles are literal. Yeah, that was very much – I go through periods of really quite terrible insomnia. And so sometimes I just get up and go and write something. So that was a 3 A.M. wake-up, this is not happening, I don’t want to read a book, I don’t want to meditate, I’m going to go and write that. And I quite like it, because it’s a little bit snaky and dream-like and odd.

Indeed. Fits the soprano really well. I noticed a subtle shift in the feel, almost like it was starting to swing, and I wondered if that was there, first of all, and was it like, does the song have a bridge?

That’s a really interesting question. It came out, when we recorded that, that was a live gig and it’s interesting, Paul Clarvis is on that one, on drums, before James Maddren joined the band. And it’s quite a different sound. And I think Paul is so heavily into the jazz tradition, he just brings that sense even if I’ve said specifically this is straight eighths, he will somehow morph. It’s not a bad thing, I mean his feel is absolutely sublime and playing swing with him is just brilliant. And yeah, it wasn’t in my mind that it would go in that direction I think.

I enjoyed the difference hearing you live, and then you have like – I call it a promo video that you have there as well. And there’s a part where you’re just in the room by yourself playing the tenor and it’s gorgeous.

Oh thank you. I think, I mean the saxophone is a fun instrument. I often – I’m often envious of piano players because they can be everything. They can be rhythmic, harmonic, kind of you know, got it all going on in a way that I suppose a one line instrument – it’s different let’s say. But it is fun when you’ve got a reed that works and an acoustic that’s really nice, then it’s fun just to see what emerges when on one’s own.
